dataset.what_one_row_represents: One college (current, defunct, or merged) of the University of Oxford, with its Wikidata ID, founding year, founder(s), namesake, motto and website.

ana_01.label: Dataset shape and missingness
ana_01.content: The dataset has 50 rows and 7 columns, one row per college. Founding years span 1201 to 2019 — 818 years. Coverage is uneven across columns: motto is almost entirely empty (49 of 50 blank; only Magdalen records 'Floreat Magdalena!'), 22 colleges have no recorded founder, 13 have no namesake, 10 have no website, and 2 colleges (Harris Manchester and St Bernard's) have no founding year at all and must be dropped from any date-based analysis. The sparsity is itself informative: Wikidata records founders and namesakes far more reliably than mottos, and the founder field is blank for nearly half the entries, often the older monastic houses whose origins are murky.

calculation.output:
rows=50 cols=7
founded_year range: 1201.0 -> 2019.0
motto missing 49, founder missing 22, named_after missing 13, website missing 10
blank founded_year: 2 -> ['Harris Manchester College', "St Bernard's College, Oxford"]

data_table.description: Missing-value count per column (out of 50 rows)

ana_02.label: Foundations per century — the two-wave shape
ana_02.content: Counting colleges by the century they were founded reveals a distinctive double-humped distribution rather than steady growth. The 13th century opens with 7 foundations, the 16th century peaks at 8 (the Reformation churn), the 18th century nearly flatlines at a single foundation, and then the 19th and 20th centuries each produce 9 — the two largest centuries in the dataset. Two colleges fall into an 'unknown' bucket because their founding year is missing. The takeaway is two great waves separated by a long quiet trough: a medieval/Tudor surge and a modern expansion, with the 18th century as the deepest valley between them.

data_table.description: Number of colleges founded per century

ana_03.label: The contested 'oldest college' trio
ana_03.content: The three oldest surviving colleges sit within 15 years of each other: University College (1249), Balliol College (1263) and Merton College (1264). Each contests the 'oldest' title on a different basis — Univ on its 1249 endowment, Balliol on continuous occupation of its site since ~1263, Merton on being first to receive statutes in 1264 — a rivalry the data alone cannot settle because all three dates are nominal and measure different things. They are preceded in the raw data only by Rewley Abbey (1201), a dissolved monastic house, and St Edmund Hall (1278) follows close behind. The clustering of the three claimants within a decade and a half is exactly why the argument is unwinnable.

calculation.output:
Rewley Abbey 1201
University College 1249 (William of Durham)
Balliol 1263 (Dervorguilla of Galloway; John I de Balliol)
Merton 1264 (Walter de Merton)
St Edmund Hall 1278
Gloucester College 1283

data_table.description: Six earliest foundations with founding year and status

ana_04.label: An 818-year span and the long Georgian gap
ana_04.content: Foundations span 818 years, from 1201 to 2019. The single largest gap before any new foundation is the 156-year silence between Worcester College (1714) and Keble College (1870) — the long 18th- and early-19th-century lull when Oxford founded essentially nothing. Other notable gaps include the 75 years before the short-lived Greek College (1699) and the 51 years before Brasenose (1509) reopened the Tudor wave. These gaps are the negative space of the two-wave story: the deepest is the Georgian trough, where over a century and a half passed between colleges.

calculation.output:
span=818 years
Keble 1870 gap=156
Greek College 1699 gap=75
Brasenose 1509 gap=51
University College 1249 gap=48
Lincoln 1427 gap=48

data_table.description: Largest gaps (years) before a new foundation

ana_05.label: Current vs defunct/merged colleges
ana_05.content: Filtering by name, 39 of the 50 colleges are current and 11 are defunct or merged. The defunct set is a roll call of Oxford's lost institutions: the monastic Rewley Abbey (1201), Gloucester (1283), Durham (1291) and Canterbury (1362) colleges dissolved at the Reformation; St Mary's (1435); Cardinal College (1525) and its successor King Henry VIII's College (1532), which were absorbed into Christ Church; the short-lived Greek College (1699); the administrative Examination Schools (1882); and Templeton College (1965), which merged into Green Templeton in 2008. This is why a naive 'oldest college' or 'average age' calculation over all 50 rows is misleading — nearly a quarter of the dataset no longer exists as a standalone college.

calculation.output:
current 39, defunct/merged 11
defunct: Rewley Abbey, Gloucester, Durham, Canterbury, St Mary's, Cardinal, King Henry VIII's, Greek, Examination Schools, Templeton, St Bernard's

ana_06.label: Founders who appear twice — the Tudor power players
ana_06.content: Of the 28 colleges with a recorded founder, there are 27 distinct individuals — nearly every founder appears only once. Just three names recur. Thomas Wolsey founded both Cardinal College and (with Henry VIII) Christ Church; Henry VIII founded King Henry VIII's College and Christ Church; and Elizabeth Wordsworth founded two women's colleges, Lady Margaret Hall and St Hugh's. Christ Church is the convergence point of the Tudor pair — it is the institution that absorbed Wolsey's and Henry's earlier failed foundations. The near-total uniqueness of founders shows that founding an Oxford college was, for almost everyone, a once-in-a-lifetime act of patronage; the three repeaters are the exceptions whose ambitions outran a single building.

calculation.output:
founders recorded: 28/50, distinct: 27
Thomas Wolsey 2, Elizabeth Wordsworth 2, Henry VIII of England 2
Wolsey: Cardinal College, Christ Church
Henry VIII: King Henry VIII's College, Christ Church

data_table.description: Founders associated with more than one college

ana_07.label: Namesakes: saints, monarchs, and the secular drift
ana_07.content: Of 37 colleges with a recorded namesake, 21 are named after a person or place and 16 after a religious figure or occasion (Mary, Jesus Christ, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity, and a roster of saints). Across eras the religious share stays roughly stable in raw counts but never overtakes the personal: pre-1600 splits 9 person/place to 8 religious, 1600–1899 splits 5 to 4, and the modern era (1900+) splits 7 to 4. The colleges named after their own founders or benefactors — Balliol, Merton, Wadham, Nuffield, Linacre, Wolfson — grow more common as religious dedication fades, tracing the slow secularisation of who Oxford chose to honour.

calculation.output:
named_after recorded: 37/50
person/place 21, religious/saint 16
by era: pre-1600 9/8, 1600-1899 5/4, modern 7/4

data_table.description: Namesake theme by era (person/place vs religious/saint)

ana_08.label: Four eras of foundation
ana_08.content: Grouping foundations into historical waves makes the rhythm explicit. The Medieval wave (1201–1499) produced 16 colleges, the Reformation era (1500–1599) produced 8 in a single compressed century, the Quiet centuries (1600–1799) produced just 4 across 200 years, and the Modern expansion (1800–2019) produced 20 — the largest wave of all, including all the women's colleges and graduate societies. The story is not gradual accumulation but bursts and droughts: two-thirds of the colleges with known dates belong to either the medieval/Tudor surge or the modern expansion, with the Georgian period almost empty between them.

ana_09.label: A website is a near-perfect survival marker
ana_09.content: The presence of a website turns out to be an almost flawless proxy for whether a college still exists. All 39 current colleges have a website. Of the 11 defunct or merged colleges, 10 have none — the sole exception is Templeton College, whose URL now redirects to Green Templeton, the college it merged into in 2008. In other words, an 800-year-old institution announces its survival through a single modern artifact: a live web address. The data accidentally encodes mortality — a dissolved medieval monastery and a 20th-century college that merged away share the same blank cell where a URL would be.

calculation.output:
current: 0 without site, 39 with site
defunct/merged: 10 without site, 1 with site (Templeton -> redirects to Green Templeton)

ana_10.label: The modern boom, decade by decade
ana_10.content: Zooming into the modern expansion (1800 onward, 20 foundations) shows it arrives in two clustered bursts rather than a smooth ramp. The 1870s alone produced 5 colleges — Keble plus the first women's colleges (Lady Margaret Hall 1878, Somerville and St Anne's 1879) — and the 1880s added 3 more. After a lull through the early 20th century, the 1960s produced another 5 (Linacre, St Catherine's, St Cross, Wolfson, Templeton), the wave of new graduate colleges. The two modern micro-booms — the 1870s admission of women and the 1960s graduate-college surge — are the engine of the dataset's second great hump.

caveats.content: Two colleges (Harris Manchester, St Bernard's) have no founding year and are excluded from all year-based analyses.
Medieval founding dates (1201/1249/1263/1264) are nominal and disputed; they should not be treated as exact.
The dataset mixes 39 current colleges with 11 defunct/merged ones; aggregate statistics over all 50 rows can mislead unless status is controlled for.
The current/defunct split is derived by name-matching against the README's named exceptions, not from a Wikidata status field.
